description: Linux kernel mechanisms behind containers (processes, memory, namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, LSM/seccomp, eBPF, filesystems, networking) and how they make or break Kubernetes node security. For platform engineers and architects preparing for CKS-level work.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.text: A process is a running program instance with its own {{c1::virtual address space}}, at least one thread, a process identifier (PID) and open file descriptors.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: What does fork() return in the parent vs the child?
notes.back: Child: 0. Parent: the child's process identifier (PID). Both continue from the instruction after fork().
notes.extra: The child starts as a near-exact copy of the parent.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: What does exec() replace, and what does it keep?
notes.back: Replaces the memory image (code, data, stack) with a new program; keeps the same process identifier (PID).
notes.analogy: fork() photocopies you; exec() gives the copy a new script to follow while it keeps the same name badge.
notes.extra: fork+exec is how shells and runtimes launch programs.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: Why doesn't fork() copy the parent's memory immediately?
notes.back: Copy-on-write: parent and child share physical pages marked read-only; a page is duplicated only when one of them writes to it.
notes.analogy: Two students share one textbook and only photocopy a page when one wants to scribble on it.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: Why is copy-on-write essential to the common fork() then exec() pattern?
notes.back: The child usually calls exec() at once and discards the memory image. Copying all parent pages would be wasted work; with copy-on-write almost nothing is copied.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: What is a zombie process?
notes.back: A terminated process whose exit status the parent hasn't collected with wait(); its process identifier (PID) and exit code linger until reaped.
notes.analogy: A guest who has checked out but whose room key nobody has collected, so the room still shows as occupied.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: What happens to an orphan process?
notes.back: It is re-parented, usually to process identifier (PID) 1 (init or the container's PID 1), which must reap it when it exits.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: A container's process identifier (PID) 1 never reaps children. What eventually fails, and which limit shows it?
notes.back: Zombies pile up and fill the PID table; once the cgroup pids.max (or the host limit) is hit, fork() fails with EAGAIN.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.text: Linux process states: running (R), sleeping (S), {{c1::uninterruptible sleep (D)}}: usually blocked on I/O and ignores even SIGKILL; stopped (T); {{c2::zombie (Z)}}: exited, not yet reaped.
notes.extra: In practice: many D processes usually mean stuck storage (e.g. a hung network file system (NFS) mount).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: What two responsibilities make process identifier (PID) 1 special?
notes.back:
• It must reap orphaned/zombie children.
  • It gets no default signal actions: an unhandled SIGTERM is simply ignored.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: Why is running a plain application as process identifier (PID) 1 in a container a problem?
notes.back: It typically ignores SIGTERM (no handler), so pods only die at the grace-period SIGKILL, and it never reaps zombies.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: A pod's entrypoint is sh -c "app" and takes the full grace period to stop. Why, and what is the fix?
notes.back: The shell is PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM to the app, so the pod only dies at SIGKILL. Fix: exec app in the script, or use a minimal init such as tini.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: What does a minimal init (tini, dumb-init) do as a container's process identifier (PID) 1?
notes.back: Forwards signals to the app (running as its child) and reaps zombies.
notes.extra: Docker: --init injects tini.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: How does Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) pick the next task to run?
notes.back: It picks the task with the lowest vruntime (virtual runtime): the leftmost node of a red-black tree of runnable tasks, i.e. the least-served task.
notes.analogy: A playground rule: whoever has had the fewest turns on the swing goes next.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: Under the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), why does a nice -20 task get more CPU than a nice 19 task?
notes.back: Nice maps to a weight: a high-weight task's vruntime grows more slowly, so it stays leftmost in the tree and is picked more often.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: What replaced Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) as Linux's default scheduler (kernel 6.6), and what does it add?
notes.back: EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First): adds eligibility and virtual deadlines to fair sharing, cutting latency for interactive tasks.
notes.extra: Older books (e.g. Linux Kernel Development) describe CFS.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: Process vs thread: what do threads share and what is private?
notes.back: Threads of one process share the address space and file descriptors; each has its own stack, registers and thread identifier (TID).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: Which syscall underlies fork(), thread creation and new namespaces on Linux?
notes.back: clone(). Its flags (CLONE_VM, CLONE_FILES, CLONE_NEWPID, …) choose what is shared, copied or newly namespaced.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.text: Nice values range from {{c1::-20 (most CPU share) to 19 (least)}}; lowering nice below the default requires {{c2::CAP_SYS_NICE}}.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::01 Processes & Scheduling
notes.front: What is a context switch, and why is it costly?
notes.back: The kernel saves one task's CPU state (registers, program counter (PC), stack pointer (SP)) and restores another's. Cost: the save/restore plus cache and translation lookaside buffer (TLB) pollution.
notes.analogy: A chef juggling orders: every switch means putting one recipe away, clearing the counter and laying out another.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: What two things does virtual memory give each process?
notes.back: A private address space (isolation from other processes) and independence from physical memory layout, which the kernel maps freely (even to disk).
notes.analogy: Hotel room numbers: every guest's key says 'room 101', but the front desk maps each to a different real room.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.text: The default page size on x86-64 is {{c1::4 KB}}; {{c2::huge pages}} (2 MB, 1 GB) reduce address-translation overhead for large allocations.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: What is a page table?
notes.back: A per-process kernel structure mapping virtual page numbers to physical frames; the memory management unit (MMU) walks it on memory access.
notes.analogy: The index at the back of a book, translating a topic (virtual page) to the actual page number (physical frame).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: What is the translation lookaside buffer (TLB), and what happens on a TLB miss?
notes.back: A small CPU cache of recent virtual→physical translations. A miss forces a (slow) page-table walk.
notes.analogy: Speed-dial for addresses: a hit skips looking the number up in the phone book.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: Minor vs major page fault?
notes.back: Minor: resolved without disk I/O (e.g. copy-on-write, page already in cache). Major: the page must be read from disk.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: What does the out of memory (OOM) killer score to choose a victim, and which per-process knob shifts that score?
notes.back: It kills the process with the highest badness score (mostly memory use); bias it via /proc/[pid]/oom_score_adj (−1000 = never kill).
notes.extra: Kubernetes sets oom_score_adj by quality of service (QoS) class: Guaranteed is protected most, BestEffort is killed first.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: How is a Kubernetes container memory limit enforced?
notes.back: As cgroup v2 memory.max. When the cgroup exceeds it and reclaim fails, the kernel OOM-kills a process in that cgroup: SIGKILL, no graceful signal.
notes.extra: Shows as OOMKilled, exit code 137.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: cgroup v2 memory.high vs memory.max?
notes.back: high: soft limit; the kernel throttles and reclaims aggressively, no kill. max: hard ceiling; exceeding it triggers the out of memory (OOM) killer.
notes.analogy: memory.high is the rumble strip on the road's edge; memory.max is the guard rail.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: Why set cgroup v2 memory.high below memory.max?
notes.back: A workload nearing its limit gets throttled and forced to reclaim memory first, which gives early warning and often avoids the out of memory (OOM) kill at memory.max.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: What is memory overcommit, and how does it fail?
notes.back: The kernel allows allocations beyond physical memory, betting not all pages get touched. Failure arrives later as an out of memory (OOM) kill, not as malloc() failing.
notes.analogy: Airline overbooking: fine until everyone actually shows up, then someone gets bumped.
notes.extra: Tuned via vm.overcommit_memory (0 heuristic, 1 always, 2 strict).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: What is a virtual memory area (VMA), and where do you see a process's VMAs?
notes.back: A contiguous virtual-memory region with uniform permissions and backing (file or anonymous). Listed in /proc/[pid]/maps.
notes.extra: maps is useful for debugging memory layout, address space layout randomization (ASLR) and what libraries are mapped.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: What does mmap() do?
notes.back: Maps a file or anonymous memory into the address space, so file I/O becomes memory access and large allocations bypass the heap allocator.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: Stack vs heap memory?
notes.back: Stack: per-thread call frames, grows/shrinks automatically. Heap: process-wide dynamic allocations, freed explicitly or by a garbage collector (GC).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::02 Memory
notes.front: In free -h, what is available vs free?
notes.back: free: unused. available: free plus reclaimable page cache. Low free but high available is healthy.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What is a Linux namespace?
notes.back: A kernel feature giving a process its own isolated instance of a global resource (process identifiers (PIDs), network stack, mounts, …). It is the core isolation mechanism behind containers.
notes.analogy: Rooms with one-way mirrors in a shared building: each room sees only its own furniture, but the building (kernel) is one.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: Mnemonic for the 8 Linux namespace types?
notes.back: PUMIC NUT: process identifier (PID), Unix time-sharing (UTS), Mount, inter-process communication (IPC), Cgroup, Net, User, Time.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does a process identifier (PID) namespace isolate?
notes.back: The process ID space: members see only processes in it (and descendants), numbered from 1. The first process becomes that namespace's PID 1.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does a network namespace isolate?
notes.back: A full network stack: interfaces, IPs, routing table, netfilter rules, port space and /proc/net. Two namespaces can both bind port 80.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does a mount namespace isolate?
notes.back: The set of visible mounts (its own view of the directory tree); mounts inside don't affect others unless propagation is configured.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does a Unix time-sharing (UTS) namespace isolate?
notes.back: Hostname and Network Information Service (NIS) domain name (from uname()), so a container can have its own hostname.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does an inter-process communication (IPC) namespace isolate?
notes.back: System V IPC objects (message queues, semaphores, shared memory) and Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) message queues.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does a user namespace do, and why is it central to rootless containers?
notes.back: It remaps user identifiers (UIDs)/group identifiers (GIDs): UID 0 inside maps to an unprivileged host UID. The container looks root inside without holding real host root.
notes.analogy: Being captain of your own boat: full authority on deck, none in the harbour master's office.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does a cgroup namespace isolate?
notes.back: The view of the cgroup hierarchy: the process sees its own cgroup as /, hiding the host's cgroup layout.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What problem does the time namespace solve?
notes.back: Per-namespace offsets for CLOCK_MONOTONIC/CLOCK_BOOTTIME, so a checkpointed/migrated container (checkpoint/restore in userspace (CRIU)) keeps consistent clocks.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: unshare() vs setns()?
notes.back: unshare(): move the caller into new namespaces. setns(): join an existing namespace via an fd (e.g. /proc/[pid]/ns/net).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: How do you run tcpdump inside a container's network namespace from the host, with no tools in the image?
notes.back: nsenter -t <pid> -n tcpdump …: joins the target process identifier (PID)'s network namespace via setns().
notes.extra: Find the PID with crictl inspect.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: How do you check whether two processes share a network namespace?
notes.back: Compare the inode of their /proc/[pid]/ns/net links (readlink): same inode = same namespace.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: In namespace terms, what is a container?
notes.back: An ordinary process placed in its own process identifier (PID), net, mount, Unix time-sharing (UTS) and inter-process communication (IPC) (usually also cgroup/user) namespaces, still on the host's shared kernel.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: Why are namespaces alone not a security boundary?
notes.back: They limit visibility only: no resource limits (cgroups), no privilege reduction (capabilities, seccomp), and the kernel is still shared.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: A container has its own network namespace but no cgroup limits. What can still go wrong for the node?
notes.back: One container can exhaust node CPU, memory, I/O or process slots (noisy neighbour or denial of service). Namespaces isolate visibility, not consumption.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: Namespaces vs chroot?
notes.back: chroot only changes the apparent filesystem root (escapable by privileged processes); namespaces isolate many resource types.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does hostNetwork: true do at the namespace level?
notes.back: The pod uses the node's network namespace: it sees real host interfaces and binds host ports.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does hostPID: true do at the namespace level?
notes.back: The pod shares the node's process identifier (PID) namespace and can see (and, with privileges, signal or ptrace) every host process.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What does hostUsers: false do for a pod?
notes.back: Gives the pod its own user namespace: root in the container maps to an unprivileged host user identifier (UID), shrinking breakout impact.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: A process escapes a pod with hostUsers: false while running as root inside it. What privilege does it have on the host?
notes.back: Only that of the unprivileged host user identifier (UID) its container root maps to. It cannot, for example, write root-owned host files.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::03 Namespaces
notes.front: What happens when process identifier (PID) 1 of a PID namespace exits?
notes.back: The kernel SIGKILLs every other process in that namespace, which is why the main process exiting ends the whole container.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: What is a cgroup?
notes.back: A kernel mechanism that groups processes to limit and account CPU, memory, block I/O and process count.
notes.analogy: A household budget envelope: each group of processes can only spend what's in its envelope.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.text: Namespaces control what a process can {{c1::see}}; cgroups control what it can {{c2::use}}.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: Key structural difference between cgroup v1 and v2?
notes.back: v1: a separate hierarchy per controller. v2: one unified hierarchy where all controllers apply to the same tree.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: Which cgroup version should current Kubernetes nodes run?
notes.back: cgroup v2 (default on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 9+, Ubuntu 22.04+); Kubernetes treats v1 as legacy (maintenance mode).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: What does cgroup v2 cpu.max mean, e.g. 50000 100000?
notes.back: Quota per period: 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms = 0.5 CPU. Over quota, the cgroup is throttled until the next period.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: Why is a container that exceeds its CPU limit throttled, while one that exceeds its memory limit is killed?
notes.back: CPU is compressible: the kernel just delays the task to the next period. Memory is incompressible: it cannot be taken back without killing something.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: At cgroup level, what do a Kubernetes CPU request and limit map to?
notes.back: Request → cpu.weight: relative share under contention, no cap. Limit → cpu.max: hard quota that throttles even on an idle node.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: What does the cgroup pids controller protect against?
notes.back: Fork bombs: pids.max caps processes/threads so one container can't exhaust the host's process identifier (PID) table.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: Who owns the cgroup v2 tree on a systemd host, and what does it hand to container runtimes?
notes.back: systemd owns the tree (slices, scopes, one cgroup per service) and delegates subtrees to runtimes so they can create child cgroups.
notes.extra: That's why kubelet and containerd should use the systemd cgroup driver.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: What is cgroup delegation?
notes.back: Handing a cgroup subtree to a less-privileged manager (e.g. a rootless runtime) so it can create child cgroups without host root.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: What does writing a process identifier (PID) to cgroup.procs do?
notes.back: Moves that process into the cgroup (cgroup.procs lists member PIDs; cgroup.threads lists thread identifiers (TIDs)).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: What does the cgroup v2 io controller limit?
notes.back: Per-device block I/O bandwidth and input/output operations per second (IOPS) (io.max), so one container can't starve others' disk access.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: How did the cgroup v1 release_agent become a container escape?
notes.back: The kernel runs release_agent as host root when a cgroup empties. With CAP_SYS_ADMIN and write access to a v1 hierarchy, a container points it at its own script and triggers it.
notes.extra: Lesson: capabilities and mounts matter as much as namespaces. cgroup v2 closes this.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::04 Cgroups
notes.front: Why does moving a node to cgroup v2 remove the release_agent escape?
notes.back: cgroup v2 has no release_agent file, so there is no kernel-run, host-root helper path for a container to hijack.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: What is a Linux capability?
notes.back: A discrete slice of root's power (about 40, e.g. bind low ports, load modules) that can be granted alone, enabling least privilege.
notes.analogy: Instead of one master key, root's keyring split into individual keys you hand out one at a time.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Why is CAP_SYS_ADMIN in a container close to host root?
notes.back: It's a huge grab-bag (mount filesystems, manipulate namespaces, …) enabling many host-level actions; it's the capability most often abused in container escapes.
notes.extra: Nicknamed "the new root".

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: What does CAP_NET_ADMIN grant?
notes.back: Network configuration: routes, interfaces, firewall rules and other network stack state.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: What does CAP_NET_RAW grant, and why drop it?
notes.back: Raw/packet sockets: sniffing and crafting (spoofed) packets. Needed by ping/tcpdump, rarely by apps.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: What does CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE grant?
notes.back: Binding to ports below 1024 without full root.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: A non-root container must listen on port 80. What is the simplest fix that adds no capability?
notes.back: Listen on a port of 1024 or above (e.g. 8080) and map it with the Service targetPort; no CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE needed.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Why is CAP_SYS_PTRACE plus hostPID: true dangerous?
notes.back: ptrace lets you inspect and inject into processes; with the host process identifier (PID) namespace, the container can attach to and manipulate host processes.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: What does CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE grant?
notes.back: Bypassing file read/write/execute permission checks (mode bits and ownership).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Why is CAP_SYS_MODULE equivalent to full host compromise?
notes.back: It loads kernel modules, i.e. arbitrary code into kernel space.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.text: Linux capability sets: effective = {{c1::what the kernel checks right now}}; permitted = {{c2::the most the process may make effective}}; bounding = {{c3::a ceiling it and its children can never exceed}}. Inheritable and ambient sets carry capabilities across execve().

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Does a container running as user identifier (UID) 0 get root's full capability set by default?
notes.back: No. Runtimes drop many (e.g. CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_MODULE, CAP_NET_ADMIN) and keep a small set (e.g. CAP_CHOWN, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: What does --privileged / privileged: true do, and why is it roughly host root?
notes.back: All capabilities, no seccomp or AppArmor/Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) confinement, and access to host devices. It removes nearly every kernel barrier, even if namespaces remain.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: How can a binary bind port 80 without being setuid root?
notes.back: Give it a file capability: setcap cap_net_bind_service+ep ./bin (inspect with getcap).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: File capability vs process capability?
notes.back: File: stored in an executable's xattr and applied on exec (like setuid). Process: the running sets (permitted/effective/…).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Which securityContext pattern implements capability least privilege?
notes.back: capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] plus a short capabilities.add list of what's truly needed.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Why is dropping capabilities more effective than only runAsNonRoot?
notes.back: runAsNonRoot only changes the user identifier (UID); a non-root process can still hold dangerous capabilities unless they are dropped.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Capabilities are dropped and the user is non-root, yet the image contains a setuid-root binary. What closes the remaining gap?
notes.back: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false (no_new_privs), so exec of setuid binaries or file-capability binaries cannot raise privileges.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Why isn't user identifier (UID) 0 inside a container automatically host root?
notes.back: Privilege is cut by dropped capabilities, and identity can be remapped by a user namespace, so "root" is constrained on both axes.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: Why aren't capabilities alone a complete sandbox?
notes.back: Single capabilities like CAP_SYS_ADMIN or CAP_SYS_MODULE enable escape by themselves; combine with namespaces, cgroups, seccomp and a Linux Security Module (LSM).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::05 Capabilities & Privilege
notes.front: What does allowPrivilegeEscalation: false set?
notes.back: The no_new_privs flag: the process and its children can't gain privileges via setuid binaries or file capabilities.
notes.analogy: A one-way ratchet on privilege: from this point it can only stay the same or go down.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: What is the Linux Security Module (LSM) framework?
notes.back: Kernel hooks at security-relevant operations (open file, create socket, …) where a pluggable mandatory access control (MAC) module (Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux), AppArmor, Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) LSM) allows or denies.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: How does Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) decide whether to allow an operation?
notes.back: It compares the subject's and object's labels (user:role:type:level) against policy, mainly by type enforcement.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.text: Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) modes: {{c1::enforcing}} blocks and logs violations; {{c2::permissive}} only logs them (for policy development); disabled is off.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: What is AppArmor's equivalent of Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) permissive mode?
notes.back: Complain mode: profile violations are logged but not blocked.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: AppArmor vs Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux): confinement model?
notes.back: AppArmor: path-based profiles per program. SELinux: label-based; every process and object has a context, regardless of path.
notes.analogy: AppArmor is a guest list by address; SELinux is a wristband system where every person and door has a colour.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.text: Default mandatory access control (MAC) by distro: Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL)/Fedora use {{c1::SELinux}}; Debian/Ubuntu use {{c2::AppArmor}}.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: Why does Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) use multi-category security (MCS) categories for containers?
notes.back: All containers share one type (e.g. container_t); a unique MCS category pair per container stops one from accessing another's files.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: Which Kubernetes securityContext field sets Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) labels?
notes.back: seLinuxOptions (user, role, type, level).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: What is Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) Linux Security Module (LSM)?
notes.back: An LSM backend letting extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) programs implement LSM hooks directly: programmable security policy without Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux)/AppArmor policy languages.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: Can seccomp and a Linux Security Module (LSM), e.g. Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) or AppArmor, run together?
notes.back: Yes: seccomp isn't an LSM and stacks with any. Minor LSMs can also stack; SELinux and AppArmor are usually exclusive as the main mandatory access control (MAC).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: What do sestatus and aa-status show?
notes.back: sestatus: Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) mode and policy. aa-status: loaded AppArmor profiles and enforce/complain state.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: What is seccomp?
notes.back: A kernel filter on which syscalls a process may make, shrinking the kernel attack surface.
notes.analogy: A bouncer at the kernel's front door holding a list of allowed requests.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: seccomp strict mode vs filter (seccomp-bpf) mode?
notes.back: Strict: only read, write, exit, sigreturn. Filter: a Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) program decides per syscall.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: What can a seccomp-bpf filter inspect, and what can't it?
notes.back: The syscall number and raw argument values. It can't dereference pointers, e.g. it can't check a file path string.
notes.extra: Actions: allow, kill, return errno, log, trap/notify.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: What does the runtime's default seccomp profile do?
notes.back: Allows several hundred common syscalls and blocks dangerous/rare ones (module loading, mount, reboot, keyring ops).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: A syscall is allowed by seccomp, but the process lacks the capability. What happens, and what does this show about the layers?
notes.back: The call still fails (typically EPERM). Capabilities, seccomp and Linux Security Modules (LSMs) are independent checks; every layer must allow the operation.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.text: Kubernetes seccompProfile.type: {{c1::RuntimeDefault}} = runtime's built-in profile; {{c2::Localhost}} = custom profile file on the node; {{c3::Unconfined}} = no filtering.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: Why does seccomp filter on syscall numbers, not libc function names?
notes.back: The syscall interface is the real user/kernel boundary; libc names are a user-space layer that doesn't exist where the filter runs.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: seccomp SCMP_ACT_KILL vs SCMP_ACT_ERRNO?
notes.back: KILL: terminate the process. ERRNO: fail the syscall with an error code the program can handle.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: Why is io_uring a challenge for seccomp?
notes.back: Operations go through shared ring buffers, not one syscall each, so seccomp can't see or filter them individually.
notes.extra: Many platforms disable or restrict io_uring for this reason.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::06 LSM & Seccomp
notes.front: What must an unprivileged process set before installing a seccomp filter, and why?
notes.back: PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS: it then can't gain privileges (e.g. via setuid) and use a filter to confuse a privileged program.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What is extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF)?
notes.back: Verified, sandboxed programs run inside the kernel at hook points, extending observability, networking and security without kernel modules.
notes.analogy: Like JavaScript for the kernel: small programs run in a sandbox at events, without rebuilding the browser.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What does the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) verifier check, and why?
notes.back: Before loading: termination, valid memory access and pointer safety, so buggy or untrusted programs can't crash or exploit the kernel.
notes.analogy: Airport security for kernel code: nothing boards until it's been scanned and proven harmless.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: If the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) verifier makes programs safe, why does loading them still need CAP_BPF or more?
notes.back: The verifier is a safety net, not a security boundary: eBPF programs can observe kernel-wide activity, and verifier bugs have been exploited. Privilege limits who may load them.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: Why couldn't early extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) programs contain unbounded loops?
notes.back: The verifier must prove termination; unbounded loops can't be proven. Loops with provable bounds are now allowed.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What is a Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) map?
notes.back: A kernel key-value structure (hash, array, ring buffer, …) for extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) state and data exchange with user space.
notes.analogy: A shared whiteboard between the kernel program and its user-space partner.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.text: extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) hook types: {{c1::kprobes/uprobes}}: dynamic hooks on almost any kernel/user function; {{c2::tracepoints}}: stable static kernel instrumentation; express data path (XDP) and traffic control (TC): network path; Linux Security Module (LSM) and cgroup hooks: security and per-cgroup events.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What is express data path (XDP)?
notes.back: An extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) hook at the earliest receive point, before the kernel allocates its packet buffer (sk_buff): very fast filtering, load balancing, distributed denial of service (DDoS) drop.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: traffic control (TC) extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) hook vs express data path (XDP)?
notes.back: TC runs later, on full packet structures: more context and handles egress too, but slower than XDP (ingress only).
notes.analogy: XDP is the guard at the factory gate; TC is the inspector on the shop floor who sees more but later.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What is extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) CO-RE?
notes.back: Compile Once, Run Everywhere: BPF Type Format (BTF) type info lets the loader fix up struct offsets per kernel, so one binary runs across versions.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What does bpftool do?
notes.back: Inspects loaded extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) programs and maps: list them, dump map contents, show attachments.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: Why was CAP_BPF introduced?
notes.back: So extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) tooling no longer needs the far broader CAP_SYS_ADMIN.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What is the Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) ring buffer for?
notes.back: Efficiently streaming events from extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) programs to user space, replacing perf buffers for most uses.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What is bpftrace?
notes.back: A high-level tracing language that compiles one-liners into extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) (kprobes/uprobes/tracepoints) without writing C.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: What is Cilium Tetragon?
notes.back: eBPF-based runtime security: observes process exec, file and network activity in-kernel and can block it in real time with low overhead.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::07 eBPF
notes.front: Falco vs Tetragon: key difference?
notes.back: Falco: rule engine on syscall events, mainly detects and alerts in user space. Tetragon: can also enforce in-kernel (kill or override) at the moment of the action.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What is the virtual file system (VFS)?
notes.back: The kernel layer giving one interface (open, read, write) over every filesystem type (ext4, XFS, overlayfs, tmpfs, …).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What does an inode hold, and what doesn't it hold?
notes.back: File metadata (size, permissions, timestamps, block pointers), but not the name; directory entries map names to inodes.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: Hard link vs symbolic link?
notes.back: Hard: another name for the same inode; data lives until the last link is gone. Symlink: a file containing a path; can cross filesystems, breaks if the target goes.
notes.analogy: A hard link is a second name on the same house's deed; a symlink is a signpost pointing to an address.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What is OverlayFS, and why do container images use it?
notes.back: A union filesystem merging read-only lowerdir layers with a writable upperdir. Many containers share base layers on disk, each with a thin writable layer.
notes.analogy: Transparent sheets on an overhead projector: you draw on the top sheet, the printed ones below stay untouched.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What is a copy-up in OverlayFS?
notes.back: Writing to a file that exists only in a lower layer first copies it into the upperdir; the write happens there.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: A container writes a 1 GB log inside its own filesystem. Where does the data live and when is it lost?
notes.back: In the OverlayFS upperdir on the node's disk; it is deleted with the container and counts toward ephemeral storage.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What is a bind mount, and which Kubernetes volume uses it?
notes.back: Making a directory or file visible at a second path without copying. hostPath volumes are bind mounts.
notes.analogy: A second door into the same room: nothing is copied, both doors lead to identical contents.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: Why do ext4 and XFS use journaling?
notes.back: Pending metadata changes are logged first, so after a crash the filesystem replays or discards them instead of a full fsck scan.
notes.analogy: Writing your to-do list before starting, so after a power cut you know exactly what was half-done.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What is tmpfs, and where does Kubernetes use it?
notes.back: A RAM-backed (swappable) filesystem, lost on unmount. Used by emptyDir with medium: Memory and /dev/shm.
notes.extra: Pitfall: its usage counts against the container's memory limit.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: Does data in a memory-backed emptyDir count against the container's memory limit?
notes.back: Yes. It is tmpfs (RAM), so filling it consumes memory charged to the cgroup, and can trigger an out of memory (OOM) kill.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What is /proc?
notes.back: A kernel-generated virtual filesystem exposing process and kernel state as files (/proc/[pid]/status, /proc/cpuinfo).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What is /sys (sysfs)?
notes.back: A virtual filesystem exposing devices, drivers and kernel objects; the cgroup interface is mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: What is a file descriptor?
notes.back: A small per-process integer handle to an open file, socket, pipe or device: the basis of "everything is a file".

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::08 Filesystems & Storage
notes.front: Why can df report more used space than du?
notes.back: df asks the filesystem; du sums files it can see. Deleted-but-still-open files (e.g. rotated logs) use space du can't see.
notes.extra: Find them: lsof +L1.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::09 Networking Internals
notes.front: What is a Linux bridge, and how do containers use it?
notes.back: A kernel L2 virtual switch. Each container's host-side veth end attaches to it (e.g. docker0); network address translation (NAT) reaches the outside.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::09 Networking Internals
notes.front: What is a veth pair, and how does it connect a container to the host?
notes.back: Two virtual Ethernet interfaces that act like a cable: a packet sent into one end comes out the other. One end sits in the container's network namespace, the other on the host (e.g. attached to a bridge).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::09 Networking Internals
notes.front: What is netfilter?
notes.back: The kernel framework of packet hook points (prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting) that iptables and nftables attach rules to.
notes.analogy: Toll booths at fixed checkpoints on the packet's road where rules can stop or rewrite traffic.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::09 Networking Internals
notes.front: What does nftables improve over iptables?
notes.back: Unified syntax for IPv4/IPv6/Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)/bridge, atomic incremental rule updates and set-based lookups that scale better.
notes.extra: Most distros' iptables binary is now iptables-nft, translating to the nftables kernel API.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::09 Networking Internals
notes.text: kube-proxy modes: {{c1::iptables}}: long-time default, now maintenance mode; {{c2::IPVS}}: deprecated in 1.35; {{c3::nftables}}: general availability (GA) in 1.33, recommended on kernel 5.13+.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::09 Networking Internals
notes.front: Why did kube-proxy's iptables mode scale poorly?
notes.back: Rule updates rewrite the whole ruleset, and packets traverse rules linearly, so update time and latency grow with Services and endpoints.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::09 Networking Internals
notes.front: How does nftables mode improve on iptables mode for kube-proxy?
notes.back: Incremental updates instead of full reloads, and set/map lookups (roughly O(1)) instead of linear rule chains. Needs kernel 5.13+.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::09 Networking Internals
notes.front: How does Cilium's extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) kube-proxy replacement avoid iptables/nftables?
notes.back: Service→endpoint mappings live in Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) maps; eBPF programs at express data path (XDP)/traffic control (TC) (or socket level) look them up and forward in constant time, with no netfilter chains.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: What is a system call?
notes.back: A defined entry point for user space to request a kernel service (open file, send data, create process), crossing the privilege boundary safely.
notes.analogy: A bank teller's window: you can't walk into the vault, but you can hand over a request slip.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: How does x86-64 Linux enter the kernel for a syscall today?
notes.back: The syscall/sysret instructions, faster than the legacy int 0x80 software interrupt.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: What is the vDSO?
notes.back: Kernel code mapped into every process so calls like clock_gettime() run in user space without a kernel transition.
notes.analogy: A self-service kiosk in the lobby: for simple requests like the time, no need to queue at the teller.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: What does strace do, and what is it built on?
notes.back: Prints every syscall a process makes (args, return values), built on ptrace().

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: What does -f add in strace -f -p <pid>?
notes.back: Also traces children created via fork()/clone().

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: strace vs ltrace?
notes.back: strace: syscalls (kernel boundary). ltrace: shared-library calls (a layer higher).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: What does yama's ptrace_scope control?
notes.back: How freely processes may ptrace unrelated processes (e.g. only their own children), blocking injection attacks.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: When a Linux system call fails, what does the C wrapper return and where does the caller find the reason?
notes.back: It returns -1 and sets the thread's errno (e.g. EPERM, ENOENT); errno is meaningful only right after the failure.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.text: To read about open() the syscall, use man section {{c1::2}}; for fopen() the C library function, section {{c2::3}}; for overviews such as capabilities(7) and namespaces(7), section {{c3::7}}.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: Where can you quickly see a process's capability sets?
notes.back: /proc/[pid]/status: CapEff, CapPrm, CapBnd (decode with capsh --decode).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: What is a signal?
notes.back: An asynchronous notification to a process (from the kernel or another process) that runs a handler or a default action (terminate, ignore, stop).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL?
notes.back: SIGTERM: a request the process can catch to clean up. SIGKILL: can't be caught, blocked or ignored; immediate.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: Why does Kubernetes send SIGTERM, then SIGKILL, when stopping a pod?
notes.back: SIGTERM allows graceful shutdown within terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 s); SIGKILL forces exit if it's still running.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: What is a race condition?
notes.back: A bug where correctness depends on the timing or interleaving of concurrent operations, usually on unsynchronized shared state.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: Mutex vs semaphore?
notes.back: Mutex: one holder, with ownership (the locker unlocks). Semaphore: a counter allowing N holders, no ownership; also used for signalling.
notes.analogy: A mutex is the single key to a bathroom; a semaphore is a bowl of N parking permits.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.text: Coffman deadlock conditions (all four required): mutual exclusion, {{c1::hold and wait}}, {{c2::no preemption}}, {{c3::circular wait}}. Break any one to prevent deadlock.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: Two threads lock mutex A then B, and B then A. Which Coffman condition does a fixed global lock order break?
notes.back: Circular wait: with one agreed order, a cycle of waiting threads cannot form.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: Anonymous pipe vs named pipe (FIFO)?
notes.back: Pipe: fds shared by related processes, no filesystem entry. FIFO: a filesystem path that unrelated processes can open.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: What is a Unix domain socket, and where do container nodes use them?
notes.back: A same-host socket addressed by a filesystem path, with the normal socket API. E.g. the container runtime interface (CRI) socket (containerd.sock) and docker.sock.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: Synchronous vs asynchronous I/O?
notes.back: Sync: the thread blocks until done. Async: the caller continues and is notified on completion, so no thread is parked per operation.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::10 Syscalls, Signals & IPC
notes.front: Why does epoll scale better than select()/poll()?
notes.back: select/poll rescan every fd on each call (O(n)); epoll keeps the interest list in the kernel and returns only ready fds.
notes.analogy: Instead of asking every guest if they need something, the waiter waits for raised hands.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: What do the two main Open Container Initiative (OCI) specifications define?
notes.back: Image Spec: the layered image format. Runtime Spec: how a runtime creates and runs a container from an on-disk bundle.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: What is runc?
notes.back: The reference Open Container Initiative (OCI) runtime: creates namespaces and cgroups, applies capabilities and seccomp/Linux Security Module (LSM), then execve()s the entrypoint.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: What is the container runtime interface (CRI)?
notes.back: The gRPC API through which the kubelet drives any compliant runtime (containerd, CRI-O) without runtime-specific code.
notes.analogy: A standard power socket: the kubelet plugs into any runtime that fits the shape.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.text: Kubernetes removed {{c1::dockershim}} in v1.24, so Docker Engine is no longer a supported node runtime (Docker-built images still run).

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Why does a container shim (e.g. containerd-shim) exist?
notes.back: It keeps the container running and holds its exit status even if containerd restarts or crashes.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Simplified: what happens at OS level when a pod's container starts?
notes.back: kubelet → container runtime interface (CRI) → containerd → shim → runc: clone() with namespace flags, set cgroup, apply caps and seccomp/Linux Security Module (LSM), execve() the entrypoint.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: How does gVisor isolate differently from runc?
notes.back: A user-space kernel intercepts the container's syscalls and reimplements most of them, passing only a small set to the host kernel.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: What does gVisor's extra isolation cost?
notes.back: Overhead on syscall-heavy workloads and compatibility gaps, since its user-space kernel reimplements only part of the Linux syscall surface.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: How does Kata Containers isolate differently from runc?
notes.back: Each pod runs in a lightweight VM with its own kernel (hardware virtualization), trading overhead and startup time for a stronger boundary.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: gVisor vs Kata: what is the extra boundary in each?
notes.back: gVisor: a syscall-emulating user-space kernel. Kata: a hardware-virtualized micro-VM with a guest kernel.
notes.extra: Both are selected per pod via a Kubernetes RuntimeClass.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Why is the shared kernel the core trust boundary for containers?
notes.back: Namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, seccomp and Linux Security Modules (LSMs) are all enforced by one host kernel; one kernel exploit (local privilege escalation (LPE)) bypasses them all. Hence gVisor/Kata for untrusted workloads.
notes.analogy: Apartments with good locks still share one foundation; crack the foundation and every apartment is exposed.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Name a threat where runc plus seccomp and Linux Security Modules (LSMs) is still weak, and the stronger option.
notes.back: A host-kernel vulnerability reachable from the container (e.g. via a permitted syscall) bypasses every kernel-enforced layer. Use gVisor or Kata for untrusted code.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: How does mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container lead to host breakout?
notes.back: The socket is full control of a root daemon: ask it to start a new container with the host's / bind-mounted. No exploit needed.
notes.analogy: Handing a stranger the remote control of the building's master-key cutting machine.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Why does mounting the runtime socket matter more than mounting a normal data directory?
notes.back: The socket is an API to a root daemon: whoever can write to it can launch privileged containers, so it equals host root.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Why is a hostPath mount of / or /etc a serious risk?
notes.back: Plain file writes to the host, e.g. cron jobs, authorized_keys or systemd units, lead to host code execution.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Name the four usual routes for a container-to-host escape.
notes.back:
• An over-broad capability (often CAP_SYS_ADMIN)
  • Host resources exposed: hostPath, hostPID/hostNetwork, runtime socket
  • A mount/cgroup misconfiguration
  • A kernel vulnerability

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Why is base-image provenance a real security control?
notes.back: Every layer can bring vulnerable or malicious code that inherits the container's privileges; scanning, signing and trusted bases cut that risk before start.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::11 Container Runtimes & Breakouts
notes.front: Why is a weakly hardened sidecar a lateral-movement path?
notes.back: Containers in a pod share the network namespace (and maybe volumes/processes), so a compromised sidecar reaches its neighbours' localhost services.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.text: systemd unit types: .service = {{c1::runs and supervises a process}}; .socket = {{c2::listens and activates a service on first connection}}; .target = {{c3::a grouping/sync point (replaces runlevels)}}; .timer = {{c4::scheduled activation (cron equivalent)}}.
notes.extra: Also: mount, automount, slice, scope.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: systemd target vs SysV runlevel?
notes.back: A runlevel is one global numbered state; a target is a named group of units with dependencies, which can be composed and depended on.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: What is journald?
notes.back: systemd's logger: captures services' stdout/stderr plus metadata in an indexed binary store, queried with journalctl.
notes.extra: Node debugging: journalctl -u kubelet.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: systemctl start vs enable?
notes.back: start: run now, this boot only. enable: start on future boots, not now. enable --now does both.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: A service is started with systemctl start and is gone after reboot. What was missed?
notes.back: systemctl enable (or enable --now): start only affects the current boot.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: What does systemd-cgtop show?
notes.back: Live top-style CPU, memory, I/O and task usage per cgroup/slice.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: How does tcpdump capture packets?
notes.back: An AF_PACKET socket receives raw frame copies, with a (classic) Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) filter in the kernel selecting what to pass up.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: What does lsof show, and why does it reveal network connections?
notes.back: Open file descriptors per process. Sockets and pipes are fds too, so it lists connections and inter-process communication (IPC) endpoints as well as files.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: What is auditd used for?
notes.back: Logging security-relevant events (chosen syscalls, file access, auth) from the kernel audit subsystem, for compliance (Center for Internet Security (CIS), Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI-DSS)) and forensics.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: Why use crictl rather than the docker CLI on a Kubernetes node?
notes.back: Nodes run container runtime interface (CRI) runtimes (containerd, CRI-O), not Docker Engine; crictl talks CRI to inspect pods, containers and images.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: What is Falco?
notes.back: A Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) runtime-security tool that evaluates syscall events (via extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF)) against rules, e.g. alerting on a shell in a container or writes to sensitive paths.
notes.analogy: A smoke detector for container behaviour: it doesn't stop the fire, it shouts.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: perf top vs perf record/report?
notes.back: top: live view of the hottest functions. record: capture samples to a file; report: analyse them afterwards.
notes.extra: perf uses hardware performance counters and tracepoints.

notes.deck: Linux Internals for Kubernetes & Security::12 systemd & Tools
notes.front: What is dmesg used for?
notes.back: Reading the kernel ring buffer: boot, driver and hardware messages, and OOM-killer reports.
